title: How the Panama Canal's locks lift ships, and why the canal depends on rain

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.title: Building the Panama Canal, 1903–1914
Explainer: how Panama Canal expansion will transform shipping once again

facts.text: A French effort to build a canal across Panama began in the 1880s and failed by the end of that decade.
Tropical diseases, mainly yellow fever and malaria, killed about 20,000 people during the French effort.
The French planned a channel at sea level; cutting such a channel through the mountains proved too difficult.
The United States took over the work in 1904 and completed the canal in 1914, after about ten years of work.
American engineers dammed the Chagres River, the main river in the canal's path, which created Gatun Lake.
Gatun Lake lies about 85 feet (26 metres) above sea level.
Three lock steps at each end of the canal raise ships to the level of Gatun Lake and later lower them back to sea level.
The locks use no pumps: water from the lake flows by gravity through underground culverts and valves into the lock chambers.
Each ship transit uses about 52 million gallons (roughly 200 million litres) of fresh water from Gatun Lake, which then flows out to the sea.
The original 1914 locks are about 110 feet wide; electric towing locomotives called mules guide ships through them with steel cables.
Larger locks opened in 2016 have basins that capture and reuse part of the water used in each transit.
Gatun Lake is refilled by rainfall over the surrounding forests.
In 2023 a drought left Gatun Lake near record lows, and from July 30 the canal cut the number of ships allowed through each day.
During the 2023 drought the queue of waiting ships grew to about 160, and waiting times rose sharply.
